title: Framework Hell, Tutorial Hell... now Skill Hell
summary: Matt Pocock names a new developer ailment: skill hell, after framework hell and tutorial hell. Skill hell is what happens when you take a pile of agent frameworks and skills - GSD, Spec Kits, BMAD, and similar - and cludge them together into one agent without a strategy, overloading the context window until the model breaks down. He admits his own skills contributed to the pile, but draws a sharp line: his skills are designed to empower the user, not the agent. The current trend of encoding whole software development processes directly into the agent removes the user from the steering wheel. His alternative: the user drives the skills, encoding personal processes into repeatable steps they understand and control - you can still delegate to an agent and even step away, but you own the loops. Punchline: from skill hell to skill hala.
what_you_learn: You learn the key architectural distinction for agent tooling: user-empowering skills versus agent-empowering frameworks, and why stuffing many skills into one context window degrades the model. This gives you a criterion for choosing and combining agent tools without blowing up your context budget.

skills.name: Context Window Management
skills.description: Skills and frameworks piled into one context window overload the model - context load is a real budget to manage.

skills.name: Agent Skill Design
skills.description: Intentionally choosing and sequencing which skills are active, instead of smacking them all into one agent.

skills.name: Multi-Agent Orchestration
skills.description: You can still hand work to an agent and step away - but you stay in control of the process and the loops.

skills.name: Workflow Design
skills.description: Turning your own development process into repeatable skills you understand, rather than adopting opaque frameworks.

skills.name: Human-in-the-Loop Collaboration
skills.description: The user keeps a hand on the steering wheel, understanding each stage and guiding the agent without babysitting it.

learnings.title: Skill hell: cludging frameworks together until the context window overloads
learnings.detail: Matt defines skill hell by analogy with framework hell and tutorial hell: developers grab frameworks like GSD, Spec Kits, and BMAD and try to cludge them all together into something that works - and it does not. The mechanism of failure is smacking a bunch of different skills into the same context window all at once, not even reading them, just checking if they work, until it overloads the model and you end up in massive context load.

learnings.title: The dividing line: skills that empower the user vs the agent
learnings.detail: Matt concedes his own skills contributed to the pile, but states his design intent: his skills empower the user, not the agent. The thing he sees people doing wrong is taking software development processes and encoding them directly into the agent, which removes the human from control. Skills should help you steer, not automate the steering.

learnings.title: Keep your hand on the steering wheel
learnings.detail: The user should be in control of the process: you understand each stage, you can guide the agent, and you do not have to stay in the loop for the whole thing. This is the human-near-the-loop stance - close enough to direct, free enough to delegate.

learnings.title: Skills encode YOUR process into repeatable steps
learnings.detail: The constructive use of skills: you encode your own processes into repeatable things you can do again and again. Rather than adopting a framework wholesale, you convert the way you actually work into skills - so you understand every stage because you designed it.

learnings.title: Context overload is the concrete failure mode of skill soup
learnings.detail: Why skill hell actually breaks things: every skill injected into the session costs context, and a pile of unexamined skills creates massive context load that degrades or confuses the model. The fix is intentional orchestration - choosing which skills are active for a given task - not maximally automating everything into the agent.

learnings.title: You can delegate to an agent and still own the loops
learnings.detail: Staying in control does not mean micromanaging: you can still delegate work to an agent and step away, but you remain in control of the process and the loops. The difference from agent-empowering frameworks is who designed the process and who can change it - you, not the framework.

key_points: Framework hell, tutorial hell - now skill hell.
Skill hell is skill soup: many frameworks and skills crammed into one context window until the model overloads.
Skills should empower the user, not the agent.
Do not encode whole dev processes into the agent - keep your hand on the steering wheel.
Skills encode YOUR process into repeatable steps you understand.
You can delegate to an agent and step away - you still own the loops.
From skill hell to skill hala.
